title: Distributed Monotone Policy Encryption with Stronger Security for DNFs and Threshold Policies from Lattices
abstract:
Distributed monotone-policy encryption (DPE) lets each user sample and publish its own key, after which anyone can encrypt to a list of published keys under a monotone access policy that determines which coalitions can decrypt. Silent threshold encryption is the $t$-out-of-$N$ special case. What makes the primitive non-trivial is compactness, where the ciphertext stays sublinear in the policy description. Every post-quantum DPE scheme so far settles for selective security, fixing the challenge policy and the corrupted positions before setup, and complexity leveraging cannot close the gap without giving up compactness. The one DPE scheme known in the stronger static model, where the policy and the placement of malicious keys are chosen adaptively, relies on witness encryption (Devadas-Jain-Waters-Wu, Asiacrypt'25).

We give the first statically secure DPE schemes from falsifiable lattice assumptions. For DNF policies, ciphertexts are of size $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda, \log N)$, independent of the number and widths of the clauses, and public keys, secret keys, and partial decryptions are of size $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda)$. For $t$-out-of-$N$ threshold policies, ciphertext of size $\tau^6 \cdot \mathsf{poly}(\lambda)$ for $\tau = \min(t^2, N - t)$, improving to $\tau^2 \cdot \mathsf{poly}(\lambda)$ given a common reference string. We prove security under decomposed LWE, and the improved threshold parameters under succinct LWE, in the random oracle model.

Our constructions generalize the equivocal encryption framework of Goyal-Yadugiri to policies. We define equivocal DPE, which simulates public keys and partial decryptions and withholds the equivocation trapdoor while releasing the public coins that accompany a ciphertext, and compiles to static DPE with no loss in parameters.

1    Introduction
Threshold encryption distributes decryption authority across a set of users: a sender encrypts to a committee,
and only an authorized coalition recovers the message. Traditional realizations fix the committee key through
a trusted dealer or an interactive distributed key-generation protocol, so the setup requires coordination,
and any change to the committee or to its access structure requires running the setup again. Silent threshold
encryption (STE) eliminates this requirement [DHMR07, DHMR08, WQZD10, RSY21, GKPW24, ADM+ 24].
Each user samples a public-secret key pair on its own and publishes the public key; a sender later selects
a committee and a threshold at encryption time, without interacting with the recipients and without any
party holding a master secret key. Asynchronous enrollment together with distributed decryption is what
makes STE attractive for committee-based protocols such as threshold-encrypted mempools [BCF+ 25], and
aligns with the ongoing effort to standardize multi-party threshold schemes [BP23].
    Distributed monotone-policy encryption (DPE) replaces the threshold predicate with a class of monotone
access policies [DJWW26, WW26]. An encryptor takes a policy P , a sequence of independently generated
public keys (pk1 , . . . , pkN ), and a message µ. Each user produces a partial decryption using its secret key,
and a collection of shares recovers µ exactly when the contributing users satisfy P . The syntax captures
distributed broadcast encryption through the 1-out-of-N policy, STE through a t-out-of-N policy, and richer
authorization rules described by monotone formulas, including DNFs. Three properties are required jointly:

   1. Silent setup: users generate keys independently, without a dealer, no key escrow, and no interactive
      key generation.
   2. Policy flexibility: the encryptor selects both the recipient keys and the access policy dynamically, and
      users generate keys without a policy in mind.
   3. Compactness: the ciphertext is sublinear in the policy description, ideally of size poly(λ, log N ).
Compactness makes DPE and its various specializations non-trivial and practically useful. Without it, one
can secret-share the message and separately encrypt a share to every relevant user, at which point the
ciphertext reproduces the size of the policy and none of the compression sought from STE or DPE remains.
The security gap and complexity-leveraging barrier. The natural security experiment lets an ad-
versary initialize honest users, supply malformed public keys of its own, corrupt honestly generated users,
request partial decryptions of chosen ciphertexts, and select the challenge policy and target recipients after
performing all such actions. The desired goal is to have the challenge message remain hidden as long as the
corrupted and maliciously generated keys do not satisfy the challenge policy. In the fully adaptive experi-
ment, corruptions and partial-decryption queries continue after the adversary sees the challenge ciphertext,
so the ciphertext itself may inform which honest users the adversary decides to corrupt later on.
    Current DPE constructions [DJWW26, CW26a, AGY26] are currently far from attaining (full) adaptive
security. The most common approach taken by the majority of prior works [RSY21, GKPW24, ADM+ 24,
WW26, CW26a, AGY26] is to establish security in a restrictive, selective security experiment. In the selective
experiment, the adversary must fix the challenge policy P together with the corrupted positions C before
seeing the system parameters. As an example, for a DNF-based access policy this means committing in
advance both to the formula and to an unsatisfying assignment that determines which wires the adversary
controls. Although the selective model does not capture real-world threats in a meaningful way, it serves as
a useful starting point to attain full adaptive security, as demonstrated by the vast literature in a variety
of advanced encryption systems [BF01, BB04, Wat05, GPSW06, Wat09, LOS+ 10, GPV08, GW09, ABB10,
CHKP10, Wat15, ABSV15, DG17b, DG17a, KMW23, GKR25, CHW25, WW26, GY26b, AMR26, GY26a].
    While the folklore ‘complexity-leveraging’ paradigm (i.e., selectively guessing the adversary’s choices)
typically suffices for upgrading a selectively secure encryption scheme to a full adaptively secure scheme
(at the cost of super-polynomial hardness assumptions), this approach fails miserably for closing the selec-
tive vs. adaptive gap for DPE schemes. The reason is that a reduction that plays against a selectively secure
challenger has to guess both the eventual policy and the eventual corruption pattern, and for a policy over
N users, there can be exponentially many admissible corruption patterns. Absorbing this loss forces the
security parameter to grow with N , which in turn makes the ciphertext grow polynomially with N . The
resulting scheme satisfies an adaptive definition as a matter of asymptotics while losing the parameter guar-
antee that made DPE worth studying; the same tension is what separates selective from adaptive security
in broadcast encryption [FN94, BGW05].
The static model. Given the large gap between selective and adaptive security notions for DPE, the com-
munity has considered an intermediate security notion called the static security model [GW09, DJWW26].1
Here the adversary sees the system parameters, initializes honestly generated public keys, supplies malicious
public keys, requests partial decryptions under honest keys, and only then chooses the challenge policy to-
gether with the assignment of honest and malicious keys to its wires. What it may not do is corrupt an
honestly generated key: adversarial control is exercised through maliciously sampled keys, and once the chal-
lenge ciphertext is out, the adversary may no longer query partial decryptions of it under honest keys. The
static model permits the adaptive choice of policy, placement of corrupt users, and their keys, but removes
user corruption queries for honestly instantiated users.
    For distributed broadcast encryption, static security is already known to sit next to adaptive security.2

Prior approaches beyond broadcast encryption. Early works designed DPE for threshold policies sat-

DPE for threshold policies from idealized algebraic models [GKPW24], for monotone formulas under pairing-
based q-type assumptions [WW26], for DNFs and sublinear threshold policies from decomposed/succinct
LWE [AGY26, CW26a], and for expressive policies from succinct witness encryption [DJWW26]. In terms
of security, nearly all prior works prove security in the selective model (or mild strengthenings generically
implied by it) [RSY21, GKPW24, ADM+ 24, WW26, AGY26, CW26a]. One notable exception is [DJWW26]
which designs a statically secure DPE scheme, but assumes witness encryption [GGSW13]. Since witness
encryption is a non-falsifiable assumption, the following is a major open question in the study of DPE:
           Can DPE for monotone policies achieve static security from a falsifiable assumption?

Outside of distributed/flexible broadcast encryption (DPE for 1-out-of-N ) [KMW23, CHW25, WW26,
GY26b, AMR26, GY26a], we do not have even a partial solution to the above.

1.1    Our Results
We answer this question affirmatively for DNF policies and threshold policies from falsifiable lattice assump-
tions. We provide two DPE constructions, one for DNFs and other for threshold policies, that are statically
secure under decomposed/succinct LWE assumption in the random oracle model. Decomposed/succinct
LWE is a falsifiable lattice assumption designed to supply the compression that q-type assumptions provide
in pairing-based cryptography [AMR25, Wee24]. We prove the following two theorems.

secure DPE scheme for DNF policies in the random oracle model. The ciphertext size is poly(λ, log N ), and
each user’s public key, secret key, and partial decryption size is poly(λ).

2     Technical Overview
Our starting point is the equivocal encryption framework of Goyal-Yadugiri [GY26b, GY26a]. The framework
splits an adaptive-looking proof into two tasks: build a fake mode that postpones every challenge-dependent
choice until the attacker reveals it, and show that the ciphertext prepared in that fake mode hides the
message. Existing formulations carry this out for broadcast encryption, where the only delayed choice is
a set of recipients. DPE delays considerably more, since the challenge consists of a policy, an assignment
of honest and adversarial public keys to its inputs, and a transcript of partial decryptions that fake mode
must keep consistent with every earlier oracle answer. We first formulate an equivocal DPE abstraction that
exposes this richer interface (Section 4.1), and then construct it for DNF policies (Section 5) and threshold
policies (Section 6).

and handles arrive. Both modes hand back the ciphertext along with the public pre-processing coins coin,

    Lifting static DPE to full adaptive security for policies beyond 1-out-of-N remains open, and the ob-
struction is worth stating. The Gentry-Waters compiler [GW09, KMW23, FWW23, HWW25] exploits a

and decide later which type shows up in the challenge. A DPE key falls into neither category. Its partial
decryption may carry prescribed information that reveals nothing on its own and yet becomes useful once
combined with other shares, so replacing such a key by an independently sampled useless one destroys the
joint distribution that reconstruction depends on. The two-key argument does not appear to extend to a
general monotone policy in a black-box way.
